contests.title: Governor
contests.summary: Leads California’s executive branch, proposes the state budget, and signs or vetoes legislation. Four-year term.

contests.title: Lieutenant Governor
contests.summary: Serves as acting governor when necessary, presides over the State Senate, and serves on state commissions and university boards. Four-year term.

contests.title: Secretary of State
contests.summary: Oversees California elections and maintains state business filings and official records. Four-year term.

contests.title: Controller
contests.summary: Serves as California’s chief fiscal officer, overseeing state accounting, payroll, audits, and unclaimed property. Four-year term.

contests.title: Treasurer
contests.summary: Manages state investments and the sale of state bonds and notes. Four-year term.

contests.title: Attorney General
contests.summary: Leads the California Department of Justice and represents the state in legal matters. Four-year term.

contests.title: Insurance Commissioner
contests.summary: Regulates insurance companies and enforces California insurance laws. Four-year term.

contests.title: Board of Equalization, District 2
contests.summary: Serves on the state tax board, overseeing county property assessments and specified state taxes. Four-year term.

contests.title: Superintendent of Public Instruction
contests.summary: Leads the California Department of Education and oversees state public-school programs. This is a nonpartisan office with a four-year term.

contests.title: Proposition 1 — Housing Affordability Bonds
contests.summary: Authorizes $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing and veterans’ home loans. The state General Fund would repay $10 billion; participating veterans would repay $1.25 billion through their mortgage payments.
contests.yes: The state could issue these bonds to fund housing programs and veterans’ home loans.
contests.no: The state could not issue these bonds. Existing housing programs would continue without this additional bond funding.
contests.noShort: Do not authorize these housing bonds.

contests.title: Proposition 2 — State Rainy Day Fund
contests.summary: Raises the required rainy day reserve target from 10% to 20% of General Fund taxes, changes how reserve deposits count toward the state spending limit, and extends required extra debt payments through 2040.
contests.yes: The state would build larger reserves and continue required extra debt payments for longer, under revised budgeting rules.
contests.no: Existing rules for state reserves, the spending limit, and extra debt payments would remain.
contests.noShort: Keep current reserve and debt-payment rules.

contests.title: Proposition 3 — Permanent Tax on High Incomes
contests.summary: Makes the existing temporary income tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of allowing it to expire in 2031. The Legislative Analyst estimates it would maintain $5 billion to $15 billion in annual revenue.
contests.yes: The higher income tax rates in place since 2012 for high-income earners would become permanent.
contests.no: The higher income tax rates would expire in 2031 as currently scheduled.
contests.yesShort: Make the existing high-income tax permanent.
contests.noShort: Let the tax increase expire in 2031.

contests.title: Proposition 4 — Public Funding of Election Campaigns
contests.summary: Repeals the ban on state and most local public campaign financing programs. New programs would have restrictions on eligible candidates and uses of funds, and could not use money earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
contests.yes: State and local governments could establish public campaign financing programs under the measure’s restrictions.
contests.no: The state and most local governments would remain prohibited from establishing these programs.
contests.noShort: Keep the existing public-financing ban.

contests.title: Proposition 5 — State Recall Election Process
contests.summary: Removes the replacement-candidate question from state recall elections. Most vacancies would be filled by appointment or a separate special election. For a recalled Governor, the Lieutenant Governor would serve, with a later election in some circumstances.
contests.yes: State recall ballots would ask only whether to remove an official, with replacements determined through the new vacancy rules.
contests.no: State recall ballots would continue to let voters choose a replacement at the same election.
contests.noShort: Keep replacement choices on recall ballots.

contests.title: Proposition 37 — Homebuyer Loan Program
contests.summary: Creates assistance for eligible middle-income buyers of newly built homes, financed with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. Homeowners’ loan payments would repay the bonds; the Legislative Analyst identifies no direct state or local costs.
contests.yes: The state would create the loan program and could issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to finance it.
contests.no: The state would not be required to create this new homebuying assistance program.
contests.yesShort: Create the bond-funded homebuyer loan program.
contests.noShort: Do not require this new loan program.

contests.title: Proposition 38 — Immunology Medical Research Bonds
contests.summary: Authorizes $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half would go to a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and half to research grants. Estimated annual repayment costs are $500 million to $600 million for about 20 years, potentially offset by research revenue.
contests.yes: The state could borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research.
contests.no: The state could not issue these research bonds.
contests.noShort: Do not authorize these research bonds.

contests.title: Proposition 39 — Government Identification for Voting
contests.summary: Requires government-issued identification for in-person voting and the last four digits of a designated identification number on mail-ballot envelopes. Also requires efforts to verify registered voters’ citizenship and provides a free state voter identification card.
contests.yes: Voters would have to provide the additional identifying information each time they vote.
contests.no: Existing voter identification and signature requirements would remain in place.
contests.noShort: Keep existing voter identification rules.

contests.title: Proposition 40 — One-Time Tax on Billionaires
contests.summary: Imposes a one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026, generally excluding real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts. Ninety percent of revenue would fund health care; the rest would fund education, food assistance, and administration.
contests.yes: The state would levy the one-time wealth tax. If Proposition 41 or 42 receives more yes votes, a court could find a conflict that prevents this measure from taking effect.
contests.no: The state would not levy this one-time wealth tax.
contests.yesShort: Levy the one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax.
contests.noShort: Do not levy this wealth tax.

contests.title: Proposition 41 — Special Tax Audits and Spending Limits
contests.summary: Requires audits before voter initiatives proposing special taxes reach the ballot and recurring audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes. It also restricts exclusions of new special-tax spending from the state spending limit.
contests.yes: The new audit and spending-limit rules would apply. If this measure receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, a court could find a conflict that prevents Proposition 40 from taking effect.
contests.no: Existing State Auditor responsibilities and state spending-limit rules would remain.
contests.yesShort: Add special-tax audits and spending-limit rules.
contests.noShort: Keep existing audit and spending-limit rules.

contests.title: Proposition 42 — Limits on Personal Property and Retroactive Taxes
contests.summary: Prohibits new state taxes on ownership of financial assets and other personal property, and limits retroactive state taxes. Conflicting taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 would be invalidated.
contests.yes: The new tax restrictions would apply. If this measure receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, a court could find a conflict that prevents Proposition 40 from taking effect.
contests.no: The state would retain its existing authority to establish taxes on personal property and enact retroactive taxes.
contests.yesShort: Restrict new personal-property and retroactive taxes.
contests.noShort: Keep the state’s existing taxing authority.

contests.title: Proposition 43 — Two-Thirds Vote for Local Special Taxes
contests.summary: Beginning January 1, 2027, raises the approval threshold for voter-proposed local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds. These taxes dedicate revenue to specified local government services.
contests.yes: Voter-proposed local special taxes would need two-thirds approval.
contests.no: These local special taxes could continue to pass with a majority vote.
contests.yesShort: Require two-thirds approval for these local taxes.
contests.noShort: Keep majority approval for these local taxes.

contests.title: Proposition 44 — Community Health Clinic Spending
contests.summary: Requires nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers to spend at least 90% of annual revenue on program services advancing their charitable purpose. Establishes penalties for noncompliance, with state enforcement costs covered by fees.
contests.yes: Affected nonprofit health clinics would have to meet the 90% program-services spending requirement.
contests.no: This new clinic spending requirement would not take effect.
contests.yesShort: Require 90% of clinic revenue for program services.
contests.noShort: Do not impose this spending requirement.

contests.title: Proposition 45 — Environmental Review Procedures
contests.summary: Changes California Environmental Quality Act procedures for eligible housing, transportation, water, health, and other projects. Sets tighter review and lawsuit deadlines and narrows what courts may consider in challenges to approvals.
contests.yes: Eligible projects could use the new environmental review and court challenge procedures.
contests.no: Projects would continue under the existing review and court challenge procedures.
contests.yesShort: Adopt new review procedures for eligible projects.
contests.noShort: Keep existing project review procedures.

contests.title: Board of Education
contests.summary: Elect three members of the San Francisco Board of Education, which sets school district policy and approves its budget. Four-year terms.

contests.title: Community College Board — Full Term
contests.summary: Elect three trustees to oversee City College of San Francisco. This contest is for full terms ending January 8, 2031; the partial term is a separate contest.

contests.title: Community College Board — Partial Term
contests.summary: Elect one City College trustee for the remainder of the term ending January 8, 2029. This is separate from the three full-term seats.

contests.title: BART Director, District 8
contests.summary: Elect the District 8 member of the BART Board of Directors, which sets transit policy, fares, and budgets. Four-year term.

contests.title: Assessor-Recorder
contests.summary: Oversees property assessments and records property documents for San Francisco. Four-year term. Uses ranked-choice voting; one candidate is listed for this office.

contests.title: Public Defender
contests.summary: Leads the office providing legal representation to people who cannot afford counsel in covered cases. Four-year term. Uses ranked-choice voting; one candidate is listed for this office.

contests.title: Regional Measure RTM — Regional Transit Measure
contests.summary: Adds a sales tax for 14 years to fund Bay Area public transit and related transportation programs: 1% in San Francisco and 0.5% in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties. Estimated revenue is $980 million annually across the five counties.
contests.yes: Approve the new sales tax, with revenues allocated to transit agencies and transportation programs under the measure’s funding formula and oversight requirements.
contests.no: Do not impose this additional regional sales tax.
contests.yesShort: Approve a 14-year regional transit sales tax; 1% in San Francisco.
contests.noShort: Do not impose this regional sales tax.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure across the five-county district to pass.

contests.title: Proposition A — Charter Changes Affecting Various City Departments and Commissions
contests.summary: Changes the City Charter to update departmental duties and procedures and eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies. Requires a commission-review task force every ten years.
contests.yes: Approve the Charter changes and require the Board of Supervisors to amend specified voter-approved laws to carry out some of them.
contests.no: Keep the existing Charter provisions and voter-approved laws covered by this measure.
contests.yesShort: Approve the departmental, procedural, and commission changes.
contests.noShort: Keep the existing provisions.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.

contests.title: Proposition B — Establishing a Municipal Finance Corporation and a Public Bank
contests.shortTitle: Prop B — Municipal Finance & Public Bank
contests.summary: Authorizes a City-owned nonprofit lending corporation if sufficient funding and resources are available. After at least three years, it could seek to become a public bank, subject to financial sustainability and regulatory approval.
contests.yes: Allow the City to establish the lending corporation and a public bank, with boards and oversight commissions specified in the measure.
contests.no: Do not grant this Charter authorization to establish the lending corporation and public bank.
contests.yesShort: Authorize a municipal finance corporation and public bank.
contests.noShort: Do not authorize them through this measure.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.

contests.title: Proposition C — Contributions to the Housing Trust Fund
contests.summary: Changes the formula for City contributions to the Housing Trust Fund to increase funding, expands eligible housing programs, and extends the fund’s expiration from 2043 to 2058. Allows temporary funding freezes or reductions under specified budget conditions.
contests.yes: Approve the new funding formula and program changes, including a higher income limit for downpayment assistance, and extend the fund to 2058.
contests.no: Keep the existing funding formula, program rules, and 2043 expiration date.
contests.yesShort: Increase and expand housing funding; extend the fund to 2058.
contests.noShort: Keep the current Housing Trust Fund rules.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.

contests.title: Proposition D — Changes to Ballot Measure Process
contests.summary: Raises the signature requirement for local initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters and raises the requirement for calling special elections. Removes the Mayor’s and a minority of supervisors’ independent power to place measures on the ballot.
contests.yes: Approve the higher signature requirements and placement changes, and allow proponents to withdraw signature initiatives until 102 days before an election. A majority of the Board could still place measures on the ballot.
contests.no: Keep current signature requirements and the existing ways for the Mayor and supervisors to place measures on the ballot.
contests.yesShort: Raise initiative requirements and change ballot-placement rules.
contests.noShort: Keep current ballot-placement rules.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.

contests.title: Proposition E — City Administrator’s Authority and Changes to City Contracting
contests.summary: Centralizes purchasing authority under the City Administrator, changes approval of purchasing rules, raises contract thresholds for Board of Supervisors review, and extends the administrator’s term from five to ten years.
contests.yes: Approve the contracting changes, including raising Board-review thresholds from $1 million to $4.5 million for revenue agreements and from $10 million to $25 million for spending contracts, with later inflation adjustments.
contests.no: Keep the existing division of contracting authority, review thresholds, and five-year administrator term.
contests.yesShort: Expand administrator authority and change contracting rules.
contests.noShort: Keep existing contracting and term rules.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.

contests.title: Proposition F — Changes to Executive Branch Management
contests.summary: Expands the Mayor’s authority over departmental responsibilities and leadership, permits deputy mayors, and allows appointing officials to remove most commissioners without cause. Specified departments and commissions are exempt.
contests.yes: Allow the Mayor to reorganize responsibilities subject to Board objection, hire deputy mayors, and hire some and fire most department heads; allow at-will removal of most commissioners by their appointing officials.
contests.no: Keep current limits on departmental reorganization, deputy mayors, and removal or appointment of department heads and commissioners.
contests.noShort: Keep the current management rules.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.

contests.title: Proposition G — Allowing Private Vehicles on the Upper Great Highway in Sunset Dunes Park
contests.summary: Would reopen the Upper Great Highway between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard to private vehicles from Monday at 4 a.m. through Friday at 6 p.m., except weekday holidays. Reopening requires necessary government approvals and permits.
contests.yes: Close Sunset Dunes Park during those weekday hours to allow private vehicles on the roadway; retain recreational use on weekends and holidays.
contests.no: Keep Sunset Dunes Park closed to private vehicles at all times, with existing access for emergency and other authorized vehicles.
contests.yesShort: Reopen the roadway to private vehicles on weekdays, except holidays.
contests.noShort: Keep the park closed to private vehicles.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.

contests.title: Proposition H — Parcel Tax to Fund Muni Operations
contests.summary: Creates an annual property parcel tax for Muni from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2042, adjusted for inflation. Rates vary with property type and size, with exemptions and senior discounts; estimated revenue is $177 million annually.
contests.yes: Approve the 15-year tax dedicated to Muni and its administration. Initial base rates include $129 for single-family parcels, $249 for multifamily parcels, and $799 for nonresidential or mixed-use parcels, plus applicable size-based charges.
contests.no: Do not create this parcel tax; Muni would continue relying on its other funding sources.
contests.yesShort: Approve a 15-year parcel tax for Muni.
contests.noShort: Do not impose this Muni parcel tax.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.

contests.title: Proposition I — Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax
contests.shortTitle: Prop I — Transfer Tax for Housing
contests.summary: Dedicates half of transfer-tax revenue from specified property transfers in the $10 million-and-up brackets to affordable housing and housing assistance, without increasing current combined rates. Adds an exemption for certain newly built multifamily property sales.
contests.yes: Create the dedicated housing tax and fund, replacing half of the current general-purpose tax in those brackets, with specified spending requirements and limits on future tax changes.
contests.no: Keep current transfer-tax rules and allow the City to continue spending that revenue for general governmental purposes.
contests.yesShort: Dedicate half of specified high-value transfer taxes to housing.
contests.noShort: Keep the current transfer-tax rules.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.

contests.title: Proposition J — Removal of Foreclosure Exemption for Real Property Transfer Tax
contests.summary: Removes the partial transfer-tax exemption for most commercial, industrial, and larger residential properties transferred to lenders through or instead of foreclosure. Starting March 1, 2027, covered transfers would be taxed on full market value.
contests.yes: Apply the existing 0.5%–6% transfer-tax rates to the full value of covered foreclosed properties. Retain the exemption for single-family homes and qualifying residential or mixed-use properties with fewer than five residential units.
contests.no: Keep the current partial exemption for transfers to lenders through or instead of foreclosure.
contests.yesShort: Remove the foreclosure tax exemption for covered properties.
contests.noShort: Keep the existing foreclosure exemption.
contests.threshold: Requires a simple majority of votes cast on the measure to pass.
